questions.question: What are React components and props — the render contract, and how does composition via children work?
questions.title: Components And Props
questions.direct_answer: A component is a FUNCTION from props to UI: (props) => element — React calls it during render, diff its output against the previous tree, and patches the DOM (the same input should describe the same UI; side effects don't belong in render). Props are the immutable INPUT — an object passed by the parent: attributes on JSX become props keys (children is just another prop: the nested elements). Props are READ-ONLY for the receiver (never mutate — the parent owns them; mutation breaks the pure-render assumption). Composition: children lets a parent wrap arbitrary content — <Card><Avatar/></Card> means Card receives the Avatar element as props.children and places it in its layout slot; this is React's替代 for inheritance — build with containment and specialization rather than class extension.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    C['component = f(props) → element'] --> TREE[JSX calls compose a tree of elements]
    TREE --> DIFF[React diffs previous vs next → patch DOM]
    P[props: parent-owned immutable input] --> C
    CH['children = just a prop: nested elements'] --> SLOT[layout slot — composition]
    EL['elements as props: actions, footer'] --> SLOT2[additional slots]
    COMP[containment + specialization] -.replaces.-> INH[class inheritance]
    MUT[mutating props] -.breaks.-> PURE[same props → same output]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why render purity is the load-bearing rule (the mechanism): React may call your component more than once per commit (StrictMode double-invoke in dev), skip it entirely (memo + same props), or re-run it after a failed commit — any of those misbehave if render has side effects (mutating props, writing to globals, firing requests as if in an event). The practical discipline: render computes UI from props/state; effects (useEffect, event handlers) do the world-interactions. When you need derived data, compute it in render (cheap) or memoize (useMemo) — never store props into state 'to modify them' (that's the copied-state anti-pattern: the copy drifts from the prop).

children mechanics (the layer beneath the syntax): props.children is whatever you nest — a single element, an ARRAY of elements (React gives keys when it flattens sibling JSX), a string, or a function (render-props: {data => <List items={data}/>} — the parent controls WHAT renders, the child controls WHERE and with what data). The function-children pattern predates hooks and is still the cleanest API for cross-cutting containers (a <Theme children={(colors) => ...}> exposes its state without re-creating a context). Alternatives to cloning: cloneElement(children, { onClick }) injects props into an existing child — powerful but opaque; the composition-friendly form is a component prop the parent passes explicitly.

The component-boundary design question (the senior close): WHEN to split a component — the split rule is one-component-one-reason-to-change, and the practical triggers are (a) the same JSX appearing twice with different data (extract for reuse), (b) a region with its own state (its own update loop), (c) a region whose complexity hides the parent's story (extract to name it — the component is a NAMED abstraction), or (d) performance isolation (memo a hot region so parent renders don't touch it). Counter-signals: prop-drilling through 5 layers and 8-props-forwarding wrappers say the boundary is in the wrong place — hoist the state or move the component down.
